tracks.name: Images & Containers
tracks.description: Package an app so it runs the same everywhere.

lessons.title: 1. Your first Dockerfile
lessons.summary: An image is a filesystem plus the command that starts it.

activities.title: Instructions, top to bottom
activities.instruction: `FROM` picks the base image, `WORKDIR` sets the working directory for later instructions, and `CMD` is the default process when a container starts.
activities.example:
FROM node:20-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY . .

RUN npm ci --omit=dev

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["node", "server.js"]

activities.title: Image vs container
activities.question: What is the relationship between an image and a container?
choices: A container is a running instance of an image
An image is a running instance of a container
activities.answer: A container is a running instance of an image
activities.explanation: The image is the built artifact — layers of files plus metadata. A container adds a writable layer and a process.

activities.title: Write a Dockerfile
activities.instruction: Write a Dockerfile that starts from `node:20-alpine`, sets `/app` as the workdir, and runs `node server.js` by default.

teaching.text: A Dockerfile is a recipe: each instruction adds a layer, and the result is an image you can run anywhere Docker is installed.

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
Use the exec form `CMD ["node", "server.js"]`. The shell form runs through `/bin/sh`, which swallows SIGTERM and delays graceful shutdown.

lessons.task: Write a Dockerfile for a Node app with a workdir and a start command.
hints: Pin a base image tag, then set where the app lives.

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
lessons.solution:
FROM node:20-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY . .

RUN npm ci --omit=dev

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["node", "server.js"]
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does the exec form of CMD make a clean shutdown easier?

lessons.title: 2. Build and run
lessons.summary: Build the image, then publish its port to the host.

activities.title: Two commands
activities.instruction: `docker build -t name .` builds from the Dockerfile in the current folder. `docker run -p host:container` maps a host port to the port the app listens on inside.
activities.example:
docker build -t shop-api .

docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 shop-api

activities.title: Port mapping
activities.question: The app listens on 3000 and you run `-p 8080:3000`. Which URL reaches it from your machine?
choices: Neither — you must use the container IP
activities.explanation: The left side is the host port, the right side the container port. Only the host side is reachable from your machine.

activities.title: Build and publish
activities.instruction: Build the current folder as `shop-api`, then run it in the background on host port 3000.

teaching.text: Building records the image locally. Running it starts a container with an isolated network namespace, so ports must be published explicitly.

docker build -t shop-api .
docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 shop-api
`--rm` deletes the container when it exits. Without it, stopped containers pile up until the disk fills.

lessons.task: Build an image and run it with port 3000 published.
hints: `-t` names the image; the trailing dot is the build context.

docker build -t shop-api .
docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 shop-api
lessons.solution:
docker build -t shop-api .

docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 shop-api
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is publishing a port required even when the app listens correctly inside the container?

lessons.title: 3. Layer caching
lessons.summary: Copy manifests, install, then copy source — so code edits don't reinstall.

activities.title: Cache invalidation is the whole game
activities.instruction: Docker caches each layer and reuses it while the instruction and its inputs are unchanged. Copying `package.json` separately keeps the install cached when only source files change.
activities.example:
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app

COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

COPY . .

CMD ["node", "server.js"]

activities.title: Which layer reruns
activities.question: With the layout above, you edit `server.js` and rebuild. What reruns?
activities.explanation: `package.json` did not change, so the install layer is still valid. `COPY . .` changes, and every layer after it reruns.

activities.title: Cache the install
activities.instruction: Write Dockerfile steps that copy the lockfile first, install with `npm ci`, then copy the rest of the source.

teaching.text: Every instruction is a cache key. Put the things that change rarely at the top and the things that change every commit at the bottom.

COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

COPY . .
`npm ci` installs exactly the lockfile and fails if it is out of sync. `npm install` may rewrite it inside the image, which is not what you want in a build.

lessons.task: Order the instructions so installing dependencies is cached.
hints: The install must come after copying only the manifests.

COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
lessons.solution:
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app

COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

COPY . .

CMD ["node", "server.js"]
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does a single `COPY . .` before `npm ci` make every code change reinstall dependencies?

lessons.title: 4. .dockerignore
lessons.summary: Keep node_modules, secrets, and git history out of the build.

activities.title: Send less to the daemon
activities.instruction: The build context is everything sent to the daemon before the build starts. `.dockerignore` trims it, which speeds the build and stops stale local state leaking into the image.

activities.title: Copying node_modules
activities.question: Why should `node_modules` be ignored in the build context?
choices: Host binaries may not match the image, and they overwrite the installed dependencies
activities.answer: Host binaries may not match the image, and they overwrite the installed dependencies
activities.explanation: Native modules are compiled per platform. A host `node_modules` can also hide a missing dependency in the Dockerfile.

activities.title: Ignore the right files
activities.instruction: Write a `.dockerignore` that excludes `node_modules`, `.env`, and `.git`.

teaching.text: Ignoring files is both a speed and a security measure. A layered image can be inspected, so an ignored `.env` never ends up in one.

node_modules
.env
.git
dist
npm-debug.log
Never pass secrets with `ARG` or `ENV` at build time — they stay in image history. Inject them at runtime.

lessons.task: Exclude node_modules, .env, and .git from the build context.
hints: One pattern per line, no commas.

node_modules
.env
.git
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is a secret passed as a build ARG still exposed after the build finishes?

tracks.name: Compose & Services
tracks.description: Run the app and its database together with one command.

lessons.title: 5. The compose file
lessons.summary: Compose describes the containers your project needs.

activities.title: One file, many containers
activities.instruction: `services:` maps a name to a container definition. `build:` points at a Dockerfile, `ports:` publishes it, and `docker compose up` starts the whole set.
activities.example:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: production

activities.title: DNS by service name
activities.question: How does the `api` service reach a service named `db` on the compose network?
activities.explanation: Compose puts all services on one network with DNS entries named after the service, so `postgres://db:5432/app` works.

activities.title: Define the api service
activities.instruction: Write a compose file with an `api` service that builds from `.` and publishes port 3000.

teaching.text: Compose is for local development and small deployments. It replaces a pile of `docker run` flags with a file you can commit.

services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
Quote port mappings. Unquoted `3000:3000` is read as a base-60 number in YAML and becomes a confusing value.

lessons.task: Define an api service that builds from the current directory.
hints: Everything sits under `services:` at two levels of indentation.

services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
lessons.solution:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: production
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does `localhost` inside a container not point at your machine?

lessons.title: 6. Adding a database
lessons.summary: The database is just another service with its own image.

activities.title: Compose the stack
activities.instruction: The `db` service uses the official `postgres` image with credentials from the environment. `depends_on` starts it before `api`, though not necessarily before it is ready to accept connections.
activities.example:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      - db
    environment:
      POSTGRES_URL: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/app
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
      POSTGRES_DB: app

activities.title: Startup order
activities.question: `depends_on: [db]` starts the db container first. Does that guarantee Postgres is ready?
choices: No — it only starts the container earlier
Yes, if the image has a healthcheck
activities.answer: No — it only starts the container earlier
activities.explanation: Start order is not readiness. Add a healthcheck with `condition: service_healthy`, or retry the connection in the app.

activities.title: Add Postgres
activities.instruction: Add a `db` service using `postgres:16-alpine` with user, password, and database set, and make `api` depend on it.

teaching.text: The database does not need a Dockerfile — official images are configured entirely through environment variables and volumes.

db:
  image: postgres:16-alpine
  environment:
    POSTGRES_USER: app
    POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    POSTGRES_DB: app
Table names, ports, and credentials in the compose file are a starting point for local work. Production needs real secrets, not committed defaults.

lessons.task: Add a Postgres service and make the api depend on it.
hints: Give the database service `image: postgres:16-alpine` and environment credentials.

depends_on:
  - db

environment:
  POSTGRES_USER: app
lessons.solution:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      - db
    environment:
      POSTGRES_URL: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/app
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
      POSTGRES_DB: app
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is start order not the same as readiness?

lessons.title: 7. Environment variables
lessons.summary: Keep configuration out of the image and load it at runtime.

activities.title: Config from outside
activities.instruction: `env_file` loads a file of key=value pairs into the container. The same image then runs in dev, staging, and production with different configuration.
activities.example:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    env_file:
      - .env
    environment:
      MONGODB_URI: mongodb://db:27017/shop

activities.title: Baked-in config
activities.question: Why not `COPY .env .env` in the Dockerfile?
choices: The file becomes part of the image and travels to every environment
activities.answer: The file becomes part of the image and travels to every environment
activities.explanation: Anything copied into an image is readable from it. Secrets then leak through registries and shared builds.

activities.title: Load the env file
activities.instruction: Configure the `api` service to load `.env` and set `MONGODB_URI` to `mongodb://db:27017/shop`.

teaching.text: Configuration belongs outside the artifact. One immutable image plus different environment variables is the whole idea behind "build once, deploy many".

env_file:
  - .env
environment:
  MONGODB_URI: mongodb://db:27017/shop
Commit `.env.example`, never `.env`. Add `.env` to both `.gitignore` and `.dockerignore`.

lessons.task: Load .env and set MONGODB_URI for the api service.
hints: `env_file` takes a list of paths.

env_file:
  - .env
environment:
  MONGODB_URI: mongodb://db:27017/shop
lessons.solution:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    env_file:
      - .env
    environment:
      MONGODB_URI: mongodb://db:27017/shop
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does copying .env into an image count as publishing the secret?

lessons.title: 8. Volumes
lessons.summary: Containers are disposable; volumes are where data survives.

activities.title: Keep the data
activities.instruction: Declare a named volume and mount it at the database's data directory. Removing and recreating the container then keeps the data intact.
activities.example:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  pgdata:

activities.title: Container removal
activities.question: You run `docker compose down` and then `up` again with the volume above. What happens to the data?
choices: It is gone with the container
It is still there — the named volume survived
It is restored from the image
activities.answer: It is still there — the named volume survived
activities.explanation: `down` removes containers, not named volumes. `down -v` is the command that deletes them.

activities.title: Persist Postgres
activities.instruction: Mount a named volume `pgdata` at `/var/lib/postgresql/data` and declare it at the top level.

teaching.text: A container's writable layer disappears with the container. A volume is storage managed by Docker, mounted into whichever container needs it.

volumes:
  - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  pgdata:
Bind mounts (`./src:/app/src`) are great for development hot reload and wrong for production, where they couple the container to host paths.

lessons.task: Mount a pgdata volume into the database.
hints: The container path comes after the colon: `pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`.

volumes:
  - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  pgdata:
lessons.solution:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  pgdata:
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What does `docker compose down -v` do that `docker compose down` does not?

tracks.name: Shipping to Production
tracks.description: Build smaller, run safer, and deploy without surprises.

lessons.title: 9. Multi-stage builds
lessons.summary: Build with dev dependencies, ship only the output.

activities.title: Two images, one Dockerfile
activities.instruction: Name the build stage, compile there, then copy only the built files into a fresh runtime stage. Dev dependencies, source maps, and the compiler never reach the final image.
activities.example:
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

activities.title: What ships
activities.question: What does the final stage of a multi-stage build contain?
choices: Only the base image plus the files you copy in
activities.answer: Only the base image plus the files you copy in
activities.explanation: Stages are independent. Nothing carries over unless you `COPY --from=build` it.

activities.title: Split build and runtime
activities.instruction: Add a `build` stage that runs `npm run build`, then copy `/app/dist` into a production stage.

teaching.text: Smaller images pull faster, start faster, and expose less. Multi-stage builds are the standard way to get there with one Dockerfile.

FROM node:20-alpine AS build
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
Copy the lockfile into the runtime stage and run `npm ci --omit=dev` there. Copying dev `node_modules` across defeats the point.

lessons.task: Use a build stage and copy only the compiled output.
hints: Name the first stage with `AS build`.

FROM node:20-alpine AS build
RUN npm run build

COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
lessons.solution:
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is copying node_modules from the build stage into the runtime stage a mistake?

lessons.title: 10. Don't run as root
lessons.summary: A container process should not be able to rewrite its own app.

activities.title: Drop privileges after copying
activities.instruction: Copy files as root, hand ownership to the built-in `node` user, then switch with `USER node`. Anything the app can exploit now runs without root inside the container.
activities.example:
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app

COPY --chown=node:node . .

USER node

CMD ["node", "server.js"]

activities.title: Root in a container
activities.question: Why does running as root inside a container still matter?
choices: It does not — containers are isolated
Container root combined with a kernel or mount escape becomes host root
activities.answer: Container root combined with a kernel or mount escape becomes host root
activities.explanation: Isolation is strong but not absolute. Least privilege limits what a container breakout can do.

activities.title: Switch to node
activities.instruction: Change the Dockerfile so the app runs as the `node` user and owns its files.

teaching.text: Most base images default to root. The official `node` image already includes an unprivileged `node` user, so switching is one line.

COPY --chown=node:node . .
USER node
If the app writes uploads or logs, create those directories and chown them before switching users, or it will fail at runtime with EACCES.

lessons.task: Run the container as the node user.
hints: `COPY --chown=node:node . .` fixes ownership without a separate chown layer.

COPY --chown=node:node . .
USER node
lessons.solution:
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app

COPY --chown=node:node . .

USER node

CMD ["node", "server.js"]
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why must writable directories be created before `USER node`?

lessons.title: 11. Healthchecks
lessons.summary: A running container is not the same as a working app.

activities.title: Ask the app if it is alive
activities.instruction: `HEALTHCHECK` runs a command inside the container on an interval and records healthy or unhealthy. `EXPOSE` documents the port; it does not publish it.
activities.example:
EXPOSE 3000

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD node -e "fetch('http://localhost:3000/health').then(r => process.exit(r.ok ? 0 : 1)).catch(() => process.exit(1))"

activities.title: EXPOSE
activities.question: What does `EXPOSE 3000` do on its own?
choices: Documents the port; publishing still needs `-p`
activities.answer: Documents the port; publishing still needs `-p`
activities.explanation: EXPOSE is metadata. Ports become reachable only when published, or when another container on the same network connects.

activities.title: Add a healthcheck
activities.instruction: Document port 3000 and add a healthcheck that fetches `/health` every 30 seconds.

teaching.text: Orchestrators restart or replace unhealthy containers. Without a healthcheck they can only see whether the process exists, not whether it serves requests.

EXPOSE 3000

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD node -e "fetch('http://localhost:3000/health').then(r => process.exit(r.ok ? 0 : 1))"
The health endpoint should check real dependencies — database included — but stay cheap. A healthcheck that queries every table will time out under load.

lessons.task: Add EXPOSE and a HEALTHCHECK hitting /health.
hints: `HEALTHCHECK CMD ...` must exit 0 for healthy.

EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s CMD node -e "fetch('http://localhost:3000/health')"
lessons.solution:
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD node -e "fetch('http://localhost:3000/health').then(r => process.exit(r.ok ? 0 : 1)).catch(() => process.exit(1))"

CMD ["node", "server.js"]
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does a container whose process is running still need a healthcheck?

lessons.title: 12. Deploying
lessons.summary: Build once, migrate, start detached, then watch the logs.

activities.title: A repeatable release
activities.instruction: Pull the built image on the server, run migrations before the new code starts, bring the stack up detached, and follow the logs. Roll back by pointing at the previous tag.
activities.example:
docker compose pull
docker compose run --rm api npm run migrate
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f api

activities.title: Migrations first
activities.question: Why run migrations before starting the new app version?
choices: New code may read columns that do not exist yet
activities.answer: New code may read columns that do not exist yet
activities.explanation: Schema changes must land before code depends on them. For zero-downtime, use backward-compatible migrations in two releases.

activities.title: Release script
activities.instruction: Write the release steps: pull images, run migrations, start the stack detached, and follow the api logs.

teaching.text: Deployment is a sequence, not a single command. The order protects the database and makes failures visible.

docker compose pull
docker compose run --rm api npm run migrate
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f api
Tag images with the commit SHA and keep the previous tag. Rolling back is then a tag change, not a rebuild under pressure.

lessons.task: Write the pull, migrate, start, and log steps for a release.
hints: Migrations run in a throwaway container: `docker compose run --rm api ...`.
docker compose run --rm api npm run migrate
lessons.solution:
docker compose pull

docker compose run --rm api npm run migrate

docker compose up -d

docker compose logs -f api
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does keeping the previous image tag make a rollback safer than rebuilding from the branch?
